Problem 9¶

This question involves the use of multiple linear regression on the Auto data set.

This dataset was used in the 1983 American Statistical Association Exposition. It includes gas mileage, horsepower, and other information for 392 vehicles.

In [410]:

import pandas as pd

Part C¶

Use the sm.OLS() function to perform a multiple linear regression with mpg as the response and all other variables except name as the predictors. Use the summarize() function to print the results. Comment on the output. For instance:

  1. Is there a relationship between the predictors and the response? Use the anova_lm() function from statsmodels to answer this question.
  2. Which predictors appear to have a statistically significant relationship to the response?
  3. What does the coefficient for the year variable suggest?

An R2 value of 0.821 indicates that 82.1% of the variability in the dataset can be explained by the model. The t-values associated with the year, origin, and weight predictors indicate that there is a significant relationship between these predictors and mpg. Additionally, the p-values associated with the t-statistic are less than 0.05, further supporting the claim that there is a significant relationship between these predictors and mpg. To further analyze these relationships, let's perform both type 1 and type 2 ANOVA tests.

Sub-Part 2¶

In [414]:
from ISLP.models import ModelSpec as MS

Type 1 ANOVA¶

In [415]:
# LINK TO REFERENCE: https://github.com/statsmodels/statsmodels/issues/8241
design = MS(predictors)
# THIS WAS FOUND HERE: https://islp.readthedocs.io/en/latest/models/spec.html
design.fit_transform(auto)
anova = sm.stats.anova_lm(*[sm.OLS(y, D).fit() for D in design.build_sequence(auto, anova_type='sequential')])
anova.index = design.names

anova

The type 1 ANOVA sequentially steps through the predictors and compares the response of each new predictor in the sequence to the previous. This is not helpful for determining the relationship between the response and predictors, as the order of the predictors in the sequence could skew their resulting response indication. A Type 2 ANOVA will be better suited for this application, as it is not dependent on the order of the predictors and assumes the predictor variables have no interaction. This will explicitly identify the predictors that have the most effect on the response.

Type 2 ANOVA¶

In [416]:
# CODE REFERENCE FOUND HERE: https://islp.readthedocs.io/en/latest/models/anova.html
dfs = []
for d in design.build_sequence(auto, anova_type='drop'):
    dfs.append(sm.stats.anova_lm(sm.OLS(y,d).fit(), model).iloc[1:])
df = pd.concat(dfs)
df.index = design.names
df

Based on the ss_diff values of 1091 and 2402 for weight and year predictors, respectively, it is clear that these predictors have the most influence on the response. Additionally, these predictors have statistically significant p-values associated with the F statistic. Statistical significance is true for the origin predictor as well, although the resulting ss_diff is not as significant as weight and year.

Part D¶

Produce some of diagnostic plots of the linear regression fit as described in the lab. Comment on any problems you see with the fit. Do the residual plots suggest any unusually large outliers? Does the leverage plot identify any observations with unusually high leverage?

In [417]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import numpy as np
In [418]:
# RESIDUALS PLOT REFERENCE LINK: https://seaborn.pydata.org/generated/seaborn.residplot.html

residuals = model.resid
fitted_values = model.fittedvalues

# Set up the plot
plt.style.use('seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid')
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 7))

# Use seaborn.residplot which creates the scatter plot and adds a LOWESS smoother
sns.residplot(
    x=fitted_values,
    y=residuals,
    lowess=True,  # This adds the LOWESS trend line
    ax=ax,
    scatter_kws={'alpha': 0.5, 'facecolors': 'lightgray', 'edgecolors': 'k'},
    line_kws={'color': 'red', 'lw': 2}
)

#Identify the outlying points, reference found here: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/6910641/how-do-i-get-indices-of-n-maximum-values-in-a-numpy-array
abs_residuals = np.absolute(residuals)
top_n = 10
top_indices = abs_residuals.nlargest(top_n).index

# Add text labels for these points
for i in top_indices:
    ax.text(fitted_values[i], residuals[i], str(i),
            horizontalalignment='left',
            verticalalignment='bottom',
            fontsize=9,
            fontweight='bold')

# Set titles and labels for clarity
ax.set_title('Residuals vs. Fitted Values', fontsize=16)
ax.set_xlabel('Fitted Values', fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel('Residuals', fontsize=12)

plt.show()

This plot exhibits heteroscedasticity, which can be corrected with a log transform. Let's do that.

In [419]:
y_log = np.log(auto['mpg'])
predictors = quantitative.drop('mpg')
log_corrected_auto = auto.copy()
for pred in predictors:
    log_corrected_auto[pred] = np.log(log_corrected_auto[pred])
x_log = sm.add_constant(log_corrected_auto[predictors])
model_log = sm.OLS(y_log, x_log, data=log_corrected_auto).fit()
print(model_log.summary())

Great, the heteroscedasticity has been corrected. The outliers seem to have changed, but this makes sense given the non-linear effect of the log transform. Data points 326 and 327 were consistently outliers in both normal and log transformed residual plots. The key outcome of the residual plots is that the model is not properly catpuring some non-linear relationships in the data, which, looking back at the scatter matrix, is expected. Weight, Horsepower, Displacement, and Acceleration are all non-linearly related to mpg, so they are likely contributing to the effect seen in the residuals plots.

Now, let's look at the leverage plot.

In [421]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 7))
fig = sm.graphics.influence_plot(model, ax=ax, criterion="cooks")

Based on this leverage plot, which utilizes Cook's for bubble scaling, data point 13 is the most influencial in the dataset. Interestingly, this point is not an outlier. It is an unusual point, but fits the model's trend well. All of the outliers identified in the residuals plots exhibit high Cook's distances, which I would expect because outliers have a disproportionate influence on the model. However, their leverage is low, implying that the model does not predict these values well, therefore they are true outliers.

Just out of curiosity, I'd like to look at the residual plots for these models. I suspect some of the relationships will be quite linear.

In [428]:
def plot_residuals(model, ax, title, x_label, y_label, outlier_count = 10):
    # RESIDUALS PLOT REFERENCE LINK: https://seaborn.pydata.org/generated/seaborn.residplot.html
    residuals = model.resid
    fitted_values = model.fittedvalues

    # Use seaborn.residplot which creates the scatter plot and adds a LOWESS smoother
    sns.residplot(
        x=fitted_values,
        y=residuals,
        lowess=True,  # This adds the LOWESS trend line
        ax=ax,
        scatter_kws={'alpha': 0.5, 'facecolors': 'lightgray', 'edgecolors': 'k'},
        line_kws={'color': 'red', 'lw': 2}
    )

    #Identify the outlying points, reference found here: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/6910641/how-do-i-get-indices-of-n-maximum-values-in-a-numpy-array
    abs_residuals = np.absolute(residuals)
    top_n = outlier_count
    top_indices = abs_residuals.nlargest(top_n).index

    # Add text labels for these points
    for i in top_indices:
        ax.text(fitted_values[i], residuals[i], str(i),
                horizontalalignment='left',
                verticalalignment='bottom',
                fontsize=9,
                fontweight='bold')

    # Set titles and labels for clarity
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=16)
    ax.set_xlabel(x_label, fontsize=12)
    ax.set_ylabel(y_label, fontsize=12)
In [429]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(18,14));

title='Residuals vs. Fitted Values'
x_label='Fitted Values'
y_label='Residuals'

plot_residuals(year_weight_model, axes[0,0], title=f'{title} (Year * Weight)', x_label=x_label, y_label=y_label);
plot_residuals(year_origin_model, axes[0,1], title=f'{title} (Year * Origin)', x_label=x_label, y_label=y_label);
plot_residuals(accel_disp_model, axes[1,0], title=f'{title} (Acceleration * Displacement)', x_label=x_label, y_label=y_label);
plot_residuals(hp_weight_model, axes[1,1], title=f'{title} (Horsepower * Weight)', x_label=x_label, y_label=y_label);

plt.show()

These residual plots are far more linear than what was seen with the model that encompassed all predictors, with the exception of Year:Weight. Based on the residual plots and R2 values, Horsepower:Weight is the most linear relationship with the most accurate model.

x_label='Fitted Values'
y_label='Residuals'

plot_residuals(model_log, axes[0], title=f'{title} (log)', x_label=x_label, y_label=y_label);
plot_residuals(model_sqrt, axes[1], title=f'{title} (sqrt)', x_label=x_label, y_label=y_label);
plot_residuals(model_square, axes[2], title=f'{title} (square)', x_label=x_label, y_label=y_label);


plt.show()

These transforms to the data impacted the models as expected. The log transform 'linearized' the data, resulting in a higher R2 value and more statistically significant predictors. The square root transform worked to remove some of the non-linearity from the data, however, it is clear that there are some polynomial relationships that could not be corrected with a square-root transformation. This is evident from the non-linear residual plot. Lastly, the square transform produced the worst R2 value, which was expected. This transform would exacerbate any interactions and non-linear behavior, and OLS is a linear model. Interestingly, in the square transform model, acceleration and cylinders became statistically significant predictors of mpg.

Part B¶

Provide an interpretation of each coefficient in the model. Be careful—some of the variables in the model are qualitative!

  1. Urban
    • Holding price and US location constant, an urban store is predicted to have sales that are, on average, 0.0219 units lower than a non-urban store. The coefficient is a per unit measure relative to Sales, therefore the average difference between urban and non-urban sales is 0.0219 per unit.
  2. US
    • Similar to Urban, a coefficient of 1.2006 indicates a unit increase of 1.2006 Sales for a 'Yes' value in the US dataset, relative to a baseline of 'No.'
  3. Price
    • A price coefficient of -0.0545 indicates that a unit price change results in 0.0545 fewer sales.

Part C¶

Write out the model in equation form, being careful to handle the qualitative variables properly.

Base MLR Formula:

y = β₀ + β₁x₁ + β₂x₂ + ... + βkxk + ε

The Urban and US variables were evaluated as binary values of 1 or 0, the equation can be modeled as seen, below:

Y = 13.0435 - (0.0219 * Urban[Yes]) + (1.2006 * US[Yes]) - 0.0545 * Price + ε

→ Y = 13.0435 - (0.0219 * 1) + (1.2006 * 1) - 0.0545 * Price + ε

This model is generally true for both Yes and No cases in Urban and US because the terms drop out when they are evaluated as No, resulting in the equation, below:

Y = 13.0435 - (0.0219 * Urban[No]) + (1.2006 * US[No]) - 0.0545 * Price + ε

→ Y = 13.0435 - (0.0219 * 0) + (1.2006 * 0) - 0.0545 * Price + ε

→ Y = 13.0435 - 0.0545 * Price + ε

NOTE: This is also true for any combination of Yes and No for Urban or US. The terms will always drop out if they are No.

Part D¶

For which of the predictors can you reject the null hypothesis H0:βj = 0?

The p-value associated with the t-statistic can be used to determine which predictors are statistically significant (i.e. the null hypothesis is rejected). Based on a significance level of 0.05, US[T.Yes] and Price are statistically significant because their p-values are 0.

Problem 14¶

This problem focuses on the collinearity problem.

Part A¶

Perform the following commands in Python:

rng = np.random.default_rng(10)
x1 = rng.uniform(0, 1, size=100)
x2 = 0.5 * x1 + rng.normal(size=100) / 10
y = 2 + 2 * x1 + 0.3 * x2 + rng.normal(size=100)

The last line corresponds to creating a linear model in which y is a function of x1 and x2. Write out the form of the linear model. What are the regression coefficients?

In [445]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(10)
x1 = rng.uniform(0, 1, size=100)
x2 = 0.5 * x1 + rng.normal(size=100) / 10
y = 2 + 2 * x1 + 0.3 * x2 + rng.normal(size=100)
In [446]:
df = pd.DataFrame({'y':list(y), 'x1':list(x1), 'x2':list(x2)})
pd.plotting.scatter_matrix(df, figsize=(15,10));

From the linear model equation, below, the form of the linear model can be determined.

y = β₀ + β₁x₁ + β₂x₂ + ... + βkxk + ε

Where:

β₀ is the intercept (2),

β₁ is the regression coefficient of x1 (2),

β₂ is the regression coefficient of x2 (0.3),

ε is the error (a randomly generated, normally distributed array of 100 observations, in this case.)

Part F¶

Do the results obtained in (c)–(e) contradict each other? Explain your answer.

There is a contradiction in parts c-e, where β2 in the original model does not reject the null hypothesis, but when x2 is modeled independently against y, β1 does reject the null hypothesis. As stated in my assessment during Part E, I suspect there is an interaction between x1 and x2. Digging deeper into this idea and referencing the original equation for x2, this hypothesis is supported. The x2 data is fundamentally a transformation of x1, which, when x1 is present, would be 'washed out' by the response between x1 and y. Additionally, the coefficients in the equation for y further amplify the input of x1 over x2, where x1 has a coefficient of 2 and x2 has a coefficient of 0.3. This effectively 'drowns out' the signal of x2 in y when x1 is present. When x2 predicts y without the influence of x1, it can do so reliably, because it is a derivative of x1, making the model a single predictor, single response equation.

Based on the impact on each of the models, this data point is a high leverage point. In ls_model, x1 is no longer a statistically significant predictor of y, instead, x2 is. This is a complete reversal from the inital dataset. Additionally, the R2 value has increased to 0.316 from 0.291 and β1 and β2 have changed from 1.6154 and 0.9428 to 0.4907 and 2.9070, respectively. In lm_model2, x1 is still a statistically significant predictor of y, but the R2 value has decreased to 0.167. In lm_model3m, x2 is still a statistically significant predictor of y, but the R2 value has increased to 0.307. To further verify my analysis, let'd take a look at the residual and leverage plots.

As I had expected, the additional observation (101) has a leverage of ~0.27 and ~0.097 in ls_model and ls_model3, respectively. In ls_model2, this observation is an outlier, which is indicative of this observation being proportionally more influencial on x2. This is also supported by the leverage plots for the respective variables.
